metadata.description: The pre-1881 Alabama Great Southern main line, Chattanooga - Wauhatchie - Trenton - Fort Payne - Attalla - Birmingham - Tuscaloosa - Eutaw - York - Meridian, drawn by operator era: the Wills Valley Railroad's Wauhatchie - Trenton stub 1862-1863; the Alabama and Chattanooga (the renamed Wills Valley) 1870-1877 north of Birmingham and 1871-1877 south of it; and the Alabama Great Southern's single proven year, 1878. The AGS from 1881 is already drawn in queen_crescent.geojson. Features of different eras share identical geometry.
metadata.colour_normalization: Rule 4: Alabama Great Southern #006747 pulled programmatically from queen_crescent.geojson's 'Alabama Great Southern: Queen & Crescent Route' feature (a compound-company feature whose colour is also the Southern Railway's green - the research report flags that the AGS and the Southern share it; kept as found, not decided here). Wills Valley Railroad #778800 and Alabama and Chattanooga Railroad #990077 are new: neither company had a colour anywhere in data/, and both hexes were checked programmatically to be unused by any feature.
metadata.ownership_splits: Three operator eras on the same track: Wills Valley 1862-1863 (Wauhatchie - Trenton only); Alabama and Chattanooga - the Wills Valley renamed on buying the North East & South West Alabama, 18 Nov 1868 - 1870/1871-1877, its 1871-1877 seizure, receiverships and trusteeships all running the trains under the A&C name and so not split; Alabama Great Southern from 1 Dec 1877. The A&C features end 1877 and the AGS features begin 1878, so no year is drawn twice.
omitted: [2] Wills Valley Wauhatchie - Trenton post-war 1865-1868: drawable NONE - no passenger year confirmed (WV1866 says only that the track was in 'comparatively fair running condition'; Chronicling America 1865-1868 found promotion and construction items only).

[6] North East & South West Alabama Meridian - York 1864-1868: drawable NONE under this railroad - the NE&SW owned no rolling stock and the trains were the Alabama & Mississippi Rivers' or the Mobile & Ohio's; belongs to a future A&MR / Selma & Meridian research item.
Wauhatchie - Trenton Aug 1863 - Apr 1865: Confederate, then U.S. Military Railroads ('Trenton Branch of the N&C') military working - not public passenger service.
Rising Fawn Iron Works Railroad (furnace spur): industrial freight, no feature.
Wauhatchie Extension Railway (1914-1917): post-era; its alignment is deliberately not drawn for these 1862-1878 features.
AGS 1877 and 1879-1880 (Chattanooga - Birmingham) and 1877, 1879-1890 (Birmingham - Meridian): no year confirmed in the research; only the 1878 [ANCHOR] is drawn.
not_yet_sourced: Start years that are the first CONFIRMED year, not the opening ([OPEN]): Alabama and Chattanooga Chattanooga - Birmingham 1870 (section openings 1869-70 undated; Wayne Cline, Alabama Railroads, 1997, and the broken-link '1870 timetable' on railga.com would date them).

Single proven years ([ANCHOR]): Alabama Great Southern Chattanooga - Birmingham 1878 and Birmingham - Meridian 1878 (Brookhaven Ledger 8 Aug 1878). An 1877, 1879 or 1880 AGS timetable would widen both; 1881-1890 on Birmingham - Meridian needs compiling from the CNO&TP / Q&C research.

Wills Valley opening: 1860 (Harrison, Wikipedia, Chattanoogan.com) vs 1861-63 (the company's 1866 reports, csa-railroads.com, Anderson); only Jan 1862 is dated. A Chattanooga Gazette or Daily Rebel item of 1860-61 would settle it.
Wills Valley post-war 1865-1868 service (an 1868 Official Guide listing of Trenton trains would make it drawable).
Whether the A&C's 1870s alignment differs from today's NS AGS line anywhere, and exactly where the 1860s-1870s Wauhatchie junction with the N&C lay.
Every headway_min and avg_speed_kmh in this file is an estimate.
source_conflicts: Wills Valley opening: Harrison p.987 '1860' vs the company's own 1866 reports (track-laying continued into the war) - drawn from the first dated evidence, 1862.
Wills Valley wartime end: company reports (Aug 1863, Bragg's order) vs Harrison/Fleming ('slight interruption throughout the war') - company reports followed.
Wauhatchie - Trenton mileage: 12 mi (Harrison, ICC) vs '20 miles from Chattanooga' (company, includes N&C trackage) vs 'about sixteen' (Anderson).
metadata.freight_only_audit: Checked at creation (2026-11-10): no freight-only years drawn. Military working of Wauhatchie - Trenton 1863-65 excluded.
metadata.horsecar_audit: Checked at creation (2026-11-10): steam from the start, no animal power.
metadata.line_label_audit: Labels written to Rule 6 at creation (2026-11-10).
metadata.interurban_audit: Checked at creation (2026-11-10): steam railroad, no interurban.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap end to end: 11.8 mi drawn vs 12 mi documented Wauhatchie - Trenton (Harrison p.987; ICC 'c.12 mi'; the company's own '20 miles from Chattanooga' includes the ~5 mi N&C trackage; Anderson's 'about sixteen' is unexplained). No straight-line leg; all on the NS AGS North District (OSM old_railway_operator=Southern) bar ~1 mi of untagged track. Waypoints Wildwood 0.1 km, Morganville 0.0 km, New England 0.0 km, Trenton 0.3 km (town centre) from the line. The Wauhatchie end is placed where the AGS runs 24 m from the CSX (ex-Nashville & Chattanooga) main at Wauhatchie Yard; the 1860s junction is not pinned more closely than that (~0.3 mi). The 1914-17 Wauhatchie Extension (the NS line north-east from here into Chattanooga) is NOT drawn. LATER ALIGNMENT: drawn on today's Norfolk Southern AGS track; whether any 1870s-1910s grade revision or relocation (Lookout Valley, Attalla, the Birmingham terminal approaches, Tuscaloosa) moved the line has NOT been checked (research report UNRESOLVED 8). This feature does not draw the Chattanooga - Wauhatchie N&C trackage its trains also used.

segments.note: The Wills Valley Railroad's 12 mi from Wauhatchie, on the Nashville & Chattanooga in Lookout Valley, south to Trenton, Dade County, Ga.; trains ran through to Chattanooga over the N&C. Start 1862 is the earliest DATED evidence of trains: the Memphis Appeal of 28 Jan 1862, quoting the Atlanta Confederacy and the company's president, reports the road 'completed to Trenton' with cars running daily between Trenton and Chattanooga. SOURCE CONFLICT on the opening, recorded not resolved: Harrison p.987 says the 12 mi were built 'in 1860' (Wikipedia and Chattanoogan.com say opened late 1860, citing nothing primary); the company's own 1866 reports say track-laying continued 'during the first two years of the war' before 'a daily train was put on'; Carl Anderson says completed 'by mid 1863'. 1860-1861 are therefore unproven and not drawn. End 1863 is a known ending: in August 1863, as Federal forces advanced, Bragg ordered the company 'to discontinue running to Trenton' and on 30 Aug 1863 sent the rolling stock to the rear (Wills Valley President's and Superintendent's reports, 1 May 1866). SOURCE CONFLICT: Harrison p.988, paraphrasing the 1873 Fleming report, says the line ran 'with slight interruption throughout the war'; the company's own nearer-the-event reports are followed. From Sept 1863 the track was worked by the U.S. Military Railroads as the 'Trenton Branch' of the N&C - military traffic, not public passenger service, not drawn. Post-war Wills Valley service 1865-1868 is unconfirmed and not drawn. Headway: the 1862 item's 'daily' cars; whether one or more trains, and whether mixed, is not stated. avg_speed_kmh is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: start from the Memphis Appeal 28 Jan 1862 (MA1862); end from the Wills Valley President's and Superintendent's reports of 1 May 1866 (WV1866); opening-date conflict from Harrison pp.984-988. Per research/branches/wills_valley_railroad.txt block [1]. avg_speed_kmh NOT sourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap end to end: 142.9 mi drawn vs c.143 mi documented Chattanooga - Birmingham (Fowler MP 338 Chattanooga, 344.0 Wauhatchie, 481.1 Birmingham; Harrison: N&C trackage Wauhatchie - Chattanooga 5.01 mi). Of this, 5.7 mi is the Nashville & Chattanooga trackage Chattanooga - Wauhatchie on today's CSX Chattanooga Subdivision (OSM old_railway_operator=L&N), and 137.2 mi Wauhatchie - Birmingham on the NS AGS North District (Fowler 137.1 mi). No straight-line leg. The 1914-17 Wauhatchie Extension into Chattanooga over the Southern is deliberately NOT used: 1870s trains entered Chattanooga over the N&C. The Chattanooga end is the nearest surviving track, ~0.9 km south of the 1858 Union Depot site (9th St & Broad), whose approach tracks are gone. Waypoints (Wildwood, Morganville, New England, Trenton, Rising Fawn, Valley Head, Fort Payne, Collinsville, Attalla, Steele, Springville, Trussville, Irondale, Birmingham) all within 0.5 km of the line. Cross-check: within 0.08 km (mean 0.01 km) of queen_crescent.geojson's AGS geometry everywhere south of Wauhatchie; north of Wauhatchie queen_crescent takes a different approach into Chattanooga (mean 0.9 km away), which this feature does not follow. LATER ALIGNMENT: drawn on today's Norfolk Southern AGS track; whether any 1870s-1910s grade revision or relocation (Lookout Valley, Attalla, the Birmingham terminal approaches, Tuscaloosa) moved the line has NOT been checked (research report UNRESOLVED 8).

segments.note: The Alabama and Chattanooga's north section, Wauhatchie - Trenton - Valley Head - Fort Payne - Attalla - Springville - Elyton (Birmingham, laid out at the A&C / South & North Alabama crossing in June 1871), with trains into Chattanooga over 5 mi of Nashville & Chattanooga trackage. The Wills Valley took the A&C name on buying the North East & South West Alabama, 18 Nov 1868 (Harrison p.995). [OPEN] START: 1870 is the first CONFIRMED year, not the opening - the 1870 Official Guide names stations as far as 'Asheville Station' (Fowler 1870G), and Robert Somers at Chattanooga, 2-5 Dec 1870, found the road 'already opened for traffic as far as Elyton' and rode it to Trenton (Somers ch. XVI); the section-by-section openings of 1869-70 are not dated, and Wauhatchie - Trenton may have run earlier (unconfirmed). Do not move the start earlier without evidence. The 1871-1877 seizure, receiverships and trusteeships (Gindrat, Walsh/Gindrat/Wofford, the U.S. Circuit Court receivers, the Stanton trustees, the Wells/Smith/Dunn special trustees, Swann for Erlanger & Co.) all ran the trains as the Alabama and Chattanooga, so they are not split (Harrison pp.1008-1028); the 1875 Official Guide lists the whole line (Fowler 'y'). End 1877 is an operator change, not a service end: the Alabama Great Southern took the road on 1 Dec 1877. The 1871 creditors' dispute stopped through trains for 'several days' in June 1871 - irrelevant at year resolution. Headway is an estimate (one train each way a day assumed; no timetable read); avg_speed_kmh is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: start from Fowler AL table 14 (1870 Official Guide station names) and Somers ch. XVI (Dec 1870); 1874-75 service from Fowler (5/1874G, 9/1874G, 'y' = 1875 Official Guide); corporate succession and receiverships from Harrison pp.995-1028. Per research/branches/wills_valley_railroad.txt block [3]. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh NOT sourced.

No straight-line leg; all on the NS AGS South District (OSM old_railway_operator=Southern). Waypoints Bessemer 0.4, Vance 0.1, Tuscaloosa 1.6 (city centre, not the depot), Moundville 0.1, Akron 0.2, Eutaw 0.5, Boligee 0.1, Livingston 0.3, York 0.1, Toomsuba 0.1, Meridian 0.3 km from the line. segments.note: The Alabama and Chattanooga's south end: Birmingham (Elyton) - Bessemer area (Jonesboro) - Tuscaloosa - Eutaw - Livingston - York - Meridian, drawn as one feature because both parts have the same confirmed start (research report blocks [4] and [5]). Meridian - Eutaw: Robert Somers, 14-15 Jan 1871, rode 'the train from Meridian' to Eutaw - 'the trains work only to Eutaw from the south-west end of the line' (Somers ch. XXII-XXIII); an A&C start on York - Eutaw in 1870 is plausible but unconfirmed (the 1870 Guide name at Russell's, Miss., is on track the Selma & Meridian also used, so it does not prove A&C trains). Eutaw - Tuscaloosa - Birmingham: the closing gap, 'some thirty-five miles on either side of Tuscaloosa' in Jan 1871, was finished 17 May 1871 (Harrison p.1007; New Orleans Republican 18 May 1871: 'will be opened for business this week'), and 'Trains will run through from Meridian to Chattanooga to-day, and regularly hereafter' (Mobile Tribune in the New Orleans Republican, 23 Jun 1871). 1871 is therefore the confirmed start over the whole of this feature; 1870 on the Meridian end is unproven and not drawn. 1875 Official Guide stops all along (Fowler 'y'). Meridian - York was the North East & South West Alabama's pre-war track, worked 1864-1868 by the Alabama & Mississippi Rivers or the Mobile & Ohio - those years are NOT this road's and are not drawn. Receiverships 1871-1877 ran the trains as the A&C (not split). End 1877 is an operator change (AGS from 1 Dec 1877), not a service end. Headway is an estimate (one train each way a day assumed; Somers: 'the railway passengers are not numerous'); avg_speed_kmh is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: Meridian - Eutaw start from Somers ch. XXII-XXIII (Jan 1871); Birmingham - Eutaw completion from Harrison p.1007 and the New Orleans Republican 18 May 1871 and 23 Jun 1871; 1875 stops from Fowler AL table 14. Per research/branches/wills_valley_railroad.txt blocks [4]-[5]. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh NOT sourced.

segments.note: [ANCHOR] 1878 is the single proven Alabama Great Southern passenger year: the Brookhaven Ledger of 8 Aug 1878 carries the AGS 'Look Out Mountain Line' advertisement - through sleeping cars between Vicksburg and Chattanooga, 'All trains pass Look Out Mountain in Daylight' - signed by the AGS general superintendent and general passenger & ticket agent, covering the whole Meridian - Chattanooga line. Service certainly ran wider both ways - the AGS operated the road from 1 Dec 1877 (ICC valuation; Harrison pp.1026-1028), the A&C ran it in 1875, and queen_crescent.geojson takes over from 1881 - but no AGS timetable or guide entry for 1877, 1879 or 1880 was found, so no other year is confirmed. Do not widen this to look plausible, and do not delete it to tidy the map. This feature draws the north half, Chattanooga (over the N&C from Wauhatchie, as until the 1917 Wauhatchie Extension) - Birmingham; same geometry as the A&C feature for 1870-1877. The AGS was organized 30 Nov 1877 by the purchasers at the A&C foreclosure (stock held by the Alabama Great Southern Railway Company, Limited, London). Headway is an estimate (the advertisement says 'all trains', i.e. more than one, but gives no times); avg_speed_kmh is an estimate.
